newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Somalis tell of atrocities by Italian troops.
newsitem.headline: Somalis tell of atrocities by Italian troops.

text.p: Nine Somalis on Wednesday told an Italian commission they either witnessed or were the victims of abuses by Italian soldiers on a U.N. mission to Somalia.
The commission led by Ettore Gallo, former president of the Italian constitutional court, heard at the Italian embassy in Addis Ababa from the Somalis flown in from Somalia's capital on Wednesday.
The hearing was in private and no details of the statements were given.

Gallo said the commission would fly to the Kenyan capital of Nairobi later on Wednesday to hear complaints from other Somalis who say they suffered at the hands of Italian troops during a U.N. mission to Somalia from late 1992 to early 1994.
The five-person inquiry commission consists of Gallo, two women, one a member of parliament and the other the president of the Jewish community in Italy, and two Italian generals.
Gallo said the inquiry commission would present its findings to Italy's government and the judiciary, which appointed it.
The public prosecutor in the Sicilian capital Palermo said in June that a former Italian soldier who accused fellow troops of killing unarmed civilians in Somalia had admitted he lied.
He said the ex-fusilier admitted fabricating evidence which was published a week earlier by the weekly magazine Panorama.
The prosecutor quoted the former soldier as saying he lied for money and three dead Somalis shown in published photographs were killed by a mine blast and not by Italian paratroopers.

Panorama published photographs showing the scane of the death of at least six civilians in a story which was part of an expose of alleged torture, rape and gratuitous killing of Somalis by Italian troops.

The allegations caused deep shock in Italy, the former colonial power in southern Somalia, and led to the establishment of four separate investigations. Two generals resigned in June, saying they wanted to speed up the investigations.
A Belgian military court acquitted on June 30 two Belgian paratroopers, saying there was insufficient evidence they maltreated a child in Somalia by swinging him over a camp fire.

An independent commission on July 2 issued a damning report on Canada's involvement in the U.N. mission, accusing the military of dishonouring its legacy and blasting the government for trying to cover it up.
After two years of testimony, the Somalia Inquiry found the torture and killing of Somali civilians reflected a lack of leadership, discipline and accountability in Canada's military.
On March 4, 1993, Canadian soldiers worried about looting shot two unarmed Somalis in the back as they fled, killing one. Twelve days later they tortured to death a 16-year-old Somali boy.
When the Canadian, Italian and Belgian troops under U.N. command were accused of atrocities, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan said he was outraged and such actions were unacceptable.

Somalia's faction leaders have demanded the United Nations pay compensation and apologise for atrocities by troops under its command. Somalia has had no central government since the fall of late dictator and president Mohamed Siad Barre in 1991.
